docs.title: Audience
docs.text: The travelers on this trip: curious adults who love the history of civilization, culture, and food.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Place key events on the route within the nine periods and compare the time between them, by answering six questions before the answers are revealed, scoring at least 5 of 6 (Bloom: Understand, verb: compare).

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Chapter 1, especially the Eras timeline and "BCE and CE Dating": the names and order of the nine periods, BCE and CE dating, and no year zero.

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Predict (5 min): Answer the six questions in order without zooming in to measure first. Note which answers surprised you.
  2. Explore (3 min): After question 6, click the events on the route and find the one closest in time to each site you most want to see.
  3. Reflect (2 min): Pick a chapter you are about to read, find its events on the timeline, and name the period each one falls in.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Exploring the timeline, zooming, and clicking events are practice, not evidence. Each question targets a misconception:

Question Misconception it tests 1. Bronze Age or Classical? The Classical period was long because it is famous. 2. Parthenon closer to Knossos or Paul? Famous ancient events are all "about the same age." 3. Byzantine or Ottoman? The Byzantine period was a short epilogue to Rome. 4. Paul before or during the Pax Romana? Placing an event inside a named span. 5. Years from 480 BCE to 330 CE? Spans across the BCE/CE line are found by subtracting. 6. When was writing almost unknown? Writing in Greece was continuous from the Bronze Age on.

docs.text:
1. Bronze Age - Wikipedia - Overview of the period, its metallurgy, and the regional chronologies behind its rounded dates.
  2. Late Bronze Age collapse - Wikipedia - The destruction of palace societies around 1200–1150 BCE and the loss of Linear B.
  3. Byzantine Empire - Wikipedia - The eastern Roman Empire from the founding of Constantinople to 1453.
  4. Year zero - Wikipedia - Why the BC/AD and BCE/CE systems have no year zero, and how astronomers number years.
  5. vis-timeline documentation - vis.js - The JavaScript library used to draw this timeline.

docs.title: Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map
docs.text: Run the Regions of the Eastern Mediterranean Map MicroSim Fullscreen

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Chapter 1 opens with a map because almost every later chapter leans on it. This MicroSim is that map, drawn like an atlas plate from Natural Earth coastlines. Only the places named in "Part One: The Map" carry labels, along with the seas and the two countries we travel through, Greece and Turkey.

Twelve places are key regions, the ones the rest of the book keeps returning to:

Kind Key regions Seas Eastern Mediterranean, Aegean Sea Straits Bosphorus, Dardanelles Land regions Thrace (European Turkey), Anatolia, Ionia, Attica and Central Greece Islands Crete, the Cyclades, the Dodecanese, the North Aegean Islands

Nine more places are labeled as context and can also be clicked: the Black Sea, the Sea of Marmara, the Ionian Sea, the Sporades, the Saronic Islands, the Ionian Islands, Cyprus, the Levant, and Egypt.

Historic regions such as Ionia and Thrace never had fixed borders, so their inland edges are drawn as dashed lines and called approximate. Their coastlines are exact.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
Explore mode (the default):

  • Hover over any region, sea, or strait to see an infobox: what kind of place it is, its other names, a one-line summary, and which of our stops are in it.
  • Click a key region to explore it. It turns olive green, gets a ✓ on the map and on the checklist, and a small burst of confetti marks the find. The detail panel below the map gives the fuller story.
  • Explore all 12 and a confetti cannon fires.
  • Can't find one? Click its name on the Checklist and the map zooms to it and makes it flash. That gives no credit: the region still has to be clicked on the map.
  • Drag to pan, and use + and − to zoom in on the islands. The mouse wheel scrolls the page as usual, not the map.

Find the Region mode hides the names of the 12 key regions and asks for them one at a time, in random order:

  • A correct click turns the region green and moves on.
  • A wrong click names the place that was clicked and gives a hint about where to look.
  • After two misses, or after pressing Show me, the answer flashes yellow and must be clicked to continue. It then counts as found, but not on the first try.
  • The score is the number found on the first try. Finishing fires the confetti cannon.

Keyboard users can Tab to each region and press Enter to click it.

docs.title: Learning Events (xAPI)
docs.text:
This MicroSim records what a student does as xAPI statements, the standard format a Learning Record Store reads. It does not send them anywhere yet.

Students never see the statements. To watch them arrive, add ?show-events=true to the URL, either the sim's own URL or the URL of a page that embeds it, such as this page. An Event stream tab then appears under the map, already open. Copy JSON copies every statement.

Verb When it is emitted What it carries initialized The map loads, or a Find challenge starts — experienced A hover of at least 0.6 seconds in Explore mode how long the hover lasted interacted A click on a region in Explore mode, or a mode change first visit or revisit, count explored asked Show me, or a click on a checklist name which region answered A click in Find mode correct or not, what was clicked, attempt number completed All 12 explored, or the Find challenge finished first-try score out of 12

Shorter hovers are treated as the mouse passing over, not as evidence, and are not recorded. The actor is always anonymous. Each statement is also announced to the page in three ways a future connection can use: a microsim:xapi window event, a postMessage to the page that embeds the iframe, and window.MicroSimEvents.statements().

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text: Locate the 12 key regions, island groups, seas, and straits of the Eastern Mediterranean on an unlabeled map (Bloom's level: Remember; verb: locate).

docs.title: Audience and Duration
docs.text: Travelers preparing for the trip, or any adult or high-school learner meeting this geography for the first time. 10–15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Read "Part One: The Map" in Chapter 1, or at least its first section, "The Eastern Mediterranean".

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (5 minutes). Hover across the map from Istanbul to Crete, reading each infobox. Then click all 12 key regions until the cannon fires. For each one, say aloud which continent it is on.
  2. Notice the straits (2 minutes). Zoom in on the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. Explain to a travel partner why whoever held these two narrow waters could "tax, feed, or starve" the cities of the Black Sea.
  3. Find the Region (5 minutes). Switch modes and find all 12 with the names hidden. Aim for at least 9 on the first try.
  4. Retry the misses. Any region marked red on the list needed a hint. Explore it once more, then play the challenge again.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text: Mastery is 9 or more of 12 found on the first try in Find the Region mode. The completed statement records that score, so an instructor connected to a Learning Record Store can see it without asking.

docs.text:
1. Eastern Mediterranean - Wikipedia - The region this map covers and the countries usually counted in it.
  2. Anatolia - Wikipedia - Name, extent, and geography of the Asian part of Turkey.
  3. Ionia - Wikipedia - The ancient Greek region on Anatolia's Aegean coast.
  4. Aegean Sea - Wikipedia - Area, boundaries, and island groups of the Aegean.
  5. Bosporus and Dardanelles - Wikipedia - The Turkish Straits.
  6. Natural Earth - public-domain map data - Source of the 1:10m country outlines, loaded through the world-atlas package.
  7. D3.js - Observable - The JavaScript library that draws the map.

docs.title: Viking Cruise Map
docs.text:
Copy this iframe to your website:

<iframe src="https://dmccreary.github.io/mediterranean-travels/sims/viking-cruise-map/main.html" width="100%" height="644px"></iframe>

Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
This map follows the Viking Star's seven-night Ancient Mediterranean Treasures voyage from Istanbul to Athens, November 14–21, 2026: the middle part of our November 11–23 trip. The cruise calls at six ports in Turkey and Greece, and the map ends with our overland day trip from Athens to Delphi:

  1. Istanbul, Turkey: Nov 14–15, overnight in port (trip days 4–5)
  2. Çanakkale, Turkey, the port for Troy and Gallipoli: Nov 16 (trip day 6)
  3. Kuşadası, Turkey, the port for Ephesus: Nov 17 (trip day 7)
  4. Rhodes, Greece: Nov 18 (trip day 8)
  5. Heraklion, Crete, Greece, the port for Knossos: Nov 19 (trip day 9)
  6. Athens (Piraeus), Greece: Nov 20, disembarking Nov 21 (trip days 10–11)
  7. Delphi, Greece, the sanctuary of Apollo and its oracle: Nov 22, a day trip by road from Athens (trip day 12)

The map labels the cruise ports by cruise day (Istanbul is cruise days 1–2) and Delphi by trip day. The daily chapters use trip days, which start with our own three days in Istanbul on November 11.

docs.title: How to Use It
docs.text:
• Step through the stops with the Next → and ← Previous buttons, the ← and → arrow keys, the numbered dots, or by clicking a numbered pin on the map. The map flies to each stop as you select it.
  • Read the stop card on the right. It shows the date, arrival and departure times, a short introduction, the key things to see, and a practical tip.
  • Follow the route. Legs already traveled are solid navy, the leg that brought you to the current stop is gold, and legs still ahead are dashed blue.
  • Click Whole route to zoom back out to the full itinerary.
  • Switch base maps with the layer control in the top-right corner of the map: street map, satellite imagery, or OpenStreetMap.

The route is approximate. The sea legs show the general track through the Dardanelles and around the islands, not the ship's exact navigation. The last leg follows the road north from Athens past Thebes and Livadeia, then up through Arachova to Delphi.

docs.title: Lesson Plan
docs.text: This map is for us as travelers, not for a classroom. Here is how to get the most from it before and during the cruise.

docs.title: What We Will Get From It
docs.text:
• A clear picture of where each port is and which waters the ship sails through to reach it.
  • The one sight at each port that matters most, and the civilization that built it.
  • A realistic plan for each shore day that fits the port's arrival and departure times.

docs.title: Before We Leave
docs.text:
1. Route tour (5 minutes). Step through all seven stops in order. At each one, notice the water the ship crosses to get there: the Sea of Marmara, the Dardanelles, the Aegean Sea, and the Sea of Crete.
  2. Choose at Çanakkale. Troy and Gallipoli lie in opposite directions, so decide in advance which story we most want to stand inside: the Bronze Age city of Homer's Iliad, or the 1915 battlefields that shaped modern Turkey, Australia, and New Zealand.
  3. Book early. Check which included excursion Viking offers at each port. The Ephesus and Knossos tours fill up first.

docs.title: Each Evening Aboard
docs.text:
1. Look ahead. Open the next port, read its card, then read that day's chapter.
  2. Plan the day. Using the arrival and departure times and the tip, sketch a schedule that gets us back to the ship at least 30 minutes before it sails.
  3. Look closer. Switch to the satellite map and zoom in on tomorrow's port. At Rhodes, find the walls of the medieval town; at Heraklion, find the Venetian fortress guarding the old harbor.

docs.title: Looking Back
docs.text:
• On the flight home, sketch the route from memory and label all six ports and Delphi.
  • Put the main sight at each port in order of age, from Knossos (about 1900 BC) to Topkapi Palace (15th century AD), and note which empire built each one.

docs.text:
1. Hagia Sophia - accessed 2026-11-10 - Wikipedia - History of Istanbul's defining monument, the first stop on the itinerary.
  2. Troy - accessed 2026-11-10 - Wikipedia - The archaeological site visited from Çanakkale.
  3. Ephesus - accessed 2026-11-10 - Wikipedia - The Greco-Roman city visited from Kuşadası.
  4. Medieval City of Rhodes - accessed 2026-11-10 - Wikipedia - The walled UNESCO old town beside the Rhodes cruise pier.
  5. Knossos - accessed 2026-11-10 - Wikipedia - The Minoan palace visited from Heraklion.
  6. Acropolis of Athens - accessed 2026-11-10 - Wikipedia - The final cruise port's main monument.
  7. Delphi - accessed 2026-11-24 - Wikipedia - The sanctuary of Apollo and its oracle, visited on a day trip from Athens.
